description: We are a team of students from Orange Coast College passionate about engineering, AI, and space exploration. With interests in hardware, software development, and emerging technologies, we're excited to collaborate, learn, and develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges!
summary: AstroLife is a guided health check-in for astronauts. It takes the astronaut from "which mission am I on?" to "what should I do next?". The astronaut picks a mission (low Earth orbit, lunar, or Mars/deep space), and NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight are ordered for that mission. That order shapes an adaptive questionnaire: urgent symptoms are screened first, and follow-up questions appear or disappear depending on the answers. A fingertip sensor (ESP32 + MAX30102) adds heart-rate and blood-oxygen estimates over USB. Deterministic Python rules turn the answers and the reading into follow-up prompts, each with simple self-care steps and a note on when to involve the crew. Every prompt is traced back to the mission, the NASA hazard and risk, the astronaut's own observation and the rule that fired. A 3D Health Compass places the findings on the body next to real NASA OSDR research. It runs offline on one computer, so the astronaut gets help even when the ground is far away. It is an educational prototype, not a medical device.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AstroLife is a desktop app that walks an astronaut through a short health check-in, then tells them what to follow up on and why.

1. Mission. The astronaut picks low Earth orbit, lunar, or Mars/deep space, and adds mission phase, mission day and whether they did a recent spacewalk (EVA).

2. Hazards. NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile and closed environments) are ordered for that mission. Each statement links to its NASA Human Research Program page and Human Research Roadmap evidence report.

3. Safety screen. Urgent symptoms come first, the same on every mission. Ticking any of them shows emergency guidance immediately.

4. Adaptive questions. One question at a time, in the order the hazards set. Answers change which follow-ups appear (for example, poor sleep adds sleep follow-ups), and each card says why it is being asked. The branching is an XState state machine, so the same answers always give the same questions.

5. Measurement. The astronaut rests a fingertip on our sensor (ESP32 + MAX30102). The firmware estimates heart rate and SpO2 and streams them over USB. AstroLife saves the median once three reports agree, and withdraws live values when the finger is removed.

6. Findings. Python rules turn the answers and the reading into follow-up prompts. Each prompt lists simple, sourced self-care steps and when to involve the crew. Each one is traced: mission → NASA hazard → NASA risk → the astronaut's observation → rule → follow-up. Measured values are colour coded against cited general references (MedlinePlus).

7. Health Compass. A 3D body shows where each prompt belongs, with recorded values and real NASA space-biology research for that region.

8. Actions and dashboard. Follow-ups can be marked done or reassessed. Everything is stored locally, and the next launch opens a dashboard with the mission, latest check-in, live values and open actions.

HOW IT USES NASA DATA

- The NASA Human Research Program hazard and risk pages and the Human Research Roadmap evidence reports decide the order of the check-in and explain every prompt.

- Radiation data is retrieved from the NASA OSDR RadLab API, validated with Pydantic, analysed with pandas and NumPy, and cached with SHA-256 checksums and full provenance. It can be retrieved again live from the app. It is labelled as historical instrument data, never as the astronaut's own exposure.

- A space-biology study (OSD-104) from the NASA OSDR Biological Data API is shown in the Health Compass for muscle health, clearly marked as research data.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

On long missions the crew cannot always reach a flight surgeon in real time. AstroLife gives a structured, repeatable check-in that adapts to the mission, catches urgent symptoms first, and turns observations into clear next steps. Every recommendation can be checked against its source, so a crew member or flight surgeon can see exactly why it appeared.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

- Hardware: ESP32 microcontroller, MAX30102 optical pulse sensor, and a custom enclosure designed by Ben Vo.

- Firmware: C++, Arduino framework, PlatformIO, SparkFun MAX3010x library.

- Backend: Python, pandas, NumPy, Pydantic, pyserial, SQLite.

- Desktop and interface: Electron, React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Motion, XState, uPlot, React Three Fiber, open-anatomy-3d.

- Testing: 197 Python tests and 144 interface tests at the last full run.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

The mission decides the order of the check-in, so a Mars crew member gets radiation and distance questions first and an ISS crew member does not. Every prompt carries its own evidence trail from NASA source to rule. The 3D Health Compass turns findings into something the astronaut can explore on a body.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty and safety: AstroLife does not diagnose and does not use machine learning or a language model to decide anything medical. Every prompt comes from a fixed rule with a source. Missing data is shown as "unassessed", never as healthy.

- Clear data labels: NASA evidence, historical research data, the astronaut's own measurements and rule-based prompts are always kept apart. A simulated sensor stream exists for demos and is labelled "simulated" everywhere, including in saved history.

- Privacy and offline use: everything stays in one local file and nothing is sent anywhere.

- Known limits: it is an educational prototype, not a medical device. The sensor's accuracy has not been compared with a reference pulse oximeter. The RadLab API does not state a unit, so the app shows "unit not stated by the API". Local history is not encrypted.
